items.stem: Which class of compound contains the –CONH₂ group?
items.answer: amides
items.markingKey: amides. Amido group.

items.stem: Why do ethanol and propan-1-ol react similarly with sodium?
options: They have the same boiling point.
They contain the same functional group.
They have the same molar mass.
items.answer: They contain the same functional group.
items.markingKey: B. Same –OH group.

items.stem: Distinguish between a carboxylic acid and an ester.
items.answer: A carboxylic acid contains –COOH (with an O–H); an ester contains –COO– linking two carbon groups and has no O–H.
items.markingKey: A carboxylic acid contains –COOH (with an O–H); an ester contains –COO– linking two carbon groups and has no O–H. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Is butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol?
items.answer: primary
items.markingKey: B. The carbon bearing the –OH is bonded to 1 other carbon atom (methanol/chloromethane count as primary).

items.stem: The compound with the condensed structural formula CH₃OCH₂CH₃ is
items.answer: an ether
items.markingKey: C. CH₃OCH₂CH₃ (methoxyethane) contains C–O–C: ether.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Classifying organic compounds by functional group is more useful than classifying them by carbon skeleton."
items.answer: Functional groups predict chemistry best, but a full description needs both classifications.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: functional group determines reactivity, so reactions can be predicted; IUPAC naming is organised around functional groups. Arguments against: carbon skeleton determines physical properties, isomerism and shape; polyfunctional molecules belong to several classes. Supported judgement: Functional groups predict chemistry best, but a full description needs both classifications.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by CH₂ and show a gradual trend in physical properties"?
items.answer: homologous series
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of homologous series.

items.stem: Explain why members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same functional group, which is the reactive part of the molecule, so they undergo the same types of reaction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have the same functional group, which is the reactive part of the molecule, so they undergo the same types of reaction. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Propanone and propanal are in the same homologous series because they have the same molecular formula." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They are functional group isomers: propanal is an aldehyde and propanone a ketone, so they belong to different series.
items.markingKey: They are functional group isomers: propanal is an aldehyde and propanone a ketone, so they belong to different series. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the boiling points of the alkanes increase with chain length.
items.answer: Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so London (dispersion) forces between molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so London (dispersion) forces between molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A member of the carboxylic acid homologous series has the molecular formula C₇H₁₄O₂. What is the molecular formula of the next member of the series?
items.answer: C₈H₁₆O₂
items.markingKey: D. Successive members differ by CH₂: C₇H₁₄O₂ + CH₂ = C₈H₁₆O₂ (general formula CₙH₂ₙO₂).

items.stem:
An unknown compound X has the percentage composition by mass: C 66.6 %, H 11.2 %, O 22.2 %. The following spectroscopic data were obtained.

Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak at m/z = 72.
Infrared spectrum: 1700–1750 cm⁻¹ (strong).
¹H NMR: 3 signals, integration ratio 3:3:2.

(a) Determine the empirical formula of X. [2]
(b) Use the mass spectrum to deduce the molecular formula of X. [1]
(c) Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of X and state what it indicates. [2]
(d) Identify the bond(s) responsible for the infrared absorptions. [1]
(e) Deduce the structure of X, explaining how the ¹H NMR data support it. [2]
items.answer: (a) C₄H₈O (b) C₄H₈O (c) 1 (d) C=O (e) butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest (M1); C₄H₈O (A1). (b) [1] Mr = 72 → C₄H₈O (A1). (c) [2] IHD = 1 (A1); one π bond or ring (A1). (d) [1] C=O (1). (e) [2] 3 environments in ratio 3:3:2 match CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (R1); structure (A1).

items.stem: Compound X, C₃H₆O, does not react with sodium but forms a yellow-orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH. (a) Draw two possible structures of X. (b) Name each and identify its class. (c) Suggest a chemical test to distinguish them. (d) Explain which has the higher boiling point.
items.answer: (a)/(b) propanal CH₃CH₂CHO (aldehyde) and propanone CH₃COCH₃ (ketone). (c) warm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ – propanal turns it orange → green, propanone no change (or Tollens’/Fehling’s). (d) similar (propanone 56 °C, propanal 48 °C) – both dipole–dipole; propanone’s more exposed C=O dipole gives slightly stronger attractions.
items.markingKey: (a)/(b) propanal CH₃CH₂CHO (aldehyde) and propanone CH₃COCH₃ (ketone). (c) warm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ – propanal turns it orange → green, propanone no change (or Tollens’/Fehling’s). (d) similar (propanone 56 °C, propanal 48 °C) – both dipole–dipole; propanone’s more exposed C=O dipole gives slightly stronger attractions.

items.stem: In a skeletal formula, which atoms are usually not drawn?
items.answer: hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon
items.markingKey: hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon. C–H hydrogens implied.

items.stem: Distinguish between propan-2-ol and propan-1-ol.
items.answer: Both C₃H₇OH: in propan-1-ol the –OH is on the end carbon (primary); in propan-2-ol it is on the middle carbon (secondary).
items.markingKey: Both C₃H₇OH: in propan-1-ol the –OH is on the end carbon (primary); in propan-2-ol it is on the middle carbon (secondary). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ should be named 1-methylpropane." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The longest chain has four carbons, so it is butane.
items.markingKey: The longest chain has four carbons, so it is butane. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: What is the molecular formula of but-2-ene?
items.answer: C₄H₈
items.markingKey: C. CH₃CH=CHCH₃ → C₄H₈.

items.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂Br?
items.answer: 1-bromopropane
items.markingKey: D. CH₃CH₂CH₂Br: halogenoalkane → 1-bromopropane.

items.stem: Name (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br.
items.answer: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane
items.markingKey: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane

items.stem: Two compounds, P and Q, both have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. P is an alcohol and Q is an alcohol. (a) Draw a structural formula and give the IUPAC name for a possible structure of P and of Q. (b) Determine the empirical formula of P. (c) State the type of isomerism shown. (d) Suggest one physical property that would differ between P and Q and explain why.
items.answer: (a) P butan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH), Q 2-methylpropan-1-ol ((CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH); (b) C₄H₁₀O; (c) structural isomerism (position/chain); (d) e.g. boiling point – different intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: (a) correct structures and names, e.g. butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol (A1 A1 A1 A1). (b) C₄H₁₀O (A1). (c) structural (chain/position) isomers (A1). (d) boiling point or solubility differs because of different intermolecular forces (e.g. hydrogen bonding in one) (R1).

items.stem:
An unknown compound X has the percentage composition by mass: C 62.0 %, H 10.4 %, O 27.5 %. The following spectroscopic data were obtained.

Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak at m/z = 58.
Infrared spectrum: 1700–1750 cm⁻¹ (strong).
¹H NMR: 1 signal, integration ratio 6 (single peak).

(a) Determine the empirical formula of X. [2]
(b) Use the mass spectrum to deduce the molecular formula of X. [1]
(c) Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of X and state what it indicates. [2]
(d) Identify the bond(s) responsible for the infrared absorptions. [1]
(e) Deduce the structure of X, explaining how the ¹H NMR data support it. [2]
items.answer: (a) C₃H₆O (b) C₃H₆O (c) 1 (d) C=O (e) propanone, CH₃COCH₃
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest (M1); C₃H₆O (A1). (b) [1] Mr = 58 → C₃H₆O (A1). (c) [2] IHD = 1 (A1); one π bond or ring (A1). (d) [1] C=O (1). (e) [2] 1 environments in ratio 6 (single peak) match CH₃COCH₃ (R1); structure (A1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "parent chain".
items.answer: The longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing the principal functional group, which gives the stem of the IUPAC name
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing the principal functional group, which gives the stem of the IUPAC name. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A formula showing the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule"?
items.answer: molecular formula
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of molecular formula.

items.stem: In "ethyl propanoate", which part of the name comes from the alcohol?
items.answer: ethyl
items.markingKey: A. Alkyl from alcohol, -oate from acid.

items.stem: Explain why "1-methylpropane" is not a valid IUPAC name.
items.answer: A methyl group on carbon 1 extends the longest chain to four carbons, so the compound is butane.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A methyl group on carbon 1 extends the longest chain to four carbons, so the compound is butane. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which is the condensed structural formula of propan-2-ol?
items.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
items.markingKey: C. propan-2-ol = CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (C₃H₈O).

items.stem: Draw the full structural formula of 2-methylpropan-2-ol and write its molecular formula.
items.answer: structure of (CH₃)₃COH; C₄H₁₀O
items.markingKey: structure of (CH₃)₃COH; C₄H₁₀O (1 each).

items.stem: Which is the condensed structural formula of pentan-3-ol?
items.answer: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
items.markingKey: D. pentan-3-ol = CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (C₅H₁₂O).

items.stem: A compound has the condensed formula CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(OH)CH₃. (a) Give its IUPAC name. (b) Draw its skeletal formula. (c) Write its molecular and empirical formulae. (d) State whether it is a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol, with a reason.
items.answer: (a) 3-methylbutan-2-ol. (b) zig-zag of four carbons with a methyl branch on C3 and OH on C2. (c) C₅H₁₂O for both. (d) secondary – the C bearing OH is bonded to two other carbons.
items.markingKey: (a) 3-methylbutan-2-ol. (b) zig-zag of four carbons with a methyl branch on C3 and OH on C2. (c) C₅H₁₂O for both. (d) secondary – the C bearing OH is bonded to two other carbons.

items.stem: "Skeletal formulae are the best way to represent organic molecules." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Skeletal formulae are the most efficient for large molecules, but full or 3D formulae are better when every atom or the spatial arrangement matters.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick to draw and read for large molecules; make the carbon skeleton and functional groups obvious; standard in research and pharmacology. Arguments against: hide hydrogen atoms, so counting H and spotting environments for NMR is harder; do not show 3D shape unless wedges/dashes are added; beginners find implied atoms confusing. Supported judgement: Skeletal formulae are the most efficient for large molecules, but full or 3D formulae are better when every atom or the spatial arrangement matters. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "racemic mixture"?
options: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarised light
The stepped line on an NMR spectrum whose heights are proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in each environment
The reciprocal of wavelength (cm⁻¹), used to locate absorptions in an infrared spectrum
A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by CH₂ and show a gradual trend in physical properties
items.answer: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarised light
items.markingKey: A. "racemic mixture" is an equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarised light.

items.stem: Explain why cis and trans isomers can have different boiling points.
items.answer: Their shapes differ: in the cis isomer the bond dipoles may not cancel, giving a net dipole and dipole–dipole forces, while the symmetric trans isomer may be non-polar.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their shapes differ: in the cis isomer the bond dipoles may not cancel, giving a net dipole and dipole–dipole forces, while the symmetric trans isomer may be non-polar. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between structural isomers and stereoisomers.
items.answer: Structural isomers differ in the bonding sequence of atoms; stereoisomers have the same bonding sequence but different spatial arrangements.
items.markingKey: Structural isomers differ in the bonding sequence of atoms; stereoisomers have the same bonding sequence but different spatial arrangements. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of 1,1-dichloroethene, 1,2-dichloroethene, hex-3-ene and pent-2-ene cannot show cis-trans isomerism?
items.answer: 1,1-dichloroethene
items.markingKey: C. 1,1-dichloroethene (CH₂=CCl₂): one C=C carbon carries two identical groups.

items.stem:
An unknown compound X has the percentage composition by mass: C 59.9 %, H 13.4 %, O 26.6 %. The following spectroscopic data were obtained.

Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak at m/z = 60.
Infrared spectrum: 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (broad), 1050–1410 cm⁻¹ (strong).
¹H NMR: 3 signals, integration ratio 6:1:1.

(a) Determine the empirical formula of X. [2]
(b) Use the mass spectrum to deduce the molecular formula of X. [1]
(c) Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of X and state what it indicates. [2]
(d) Identify the bond(s) responsible for the infrared absorptions. [1]
(e) Deduce the structure of X, explaining how the ¹H NMR data support it. [2]
items.answer: (a) C₃H₈O (b) C₃H₈O (c) 0 (d) O–H (alcohols), C–O (e) propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest (M1); C₃H₈O (A1). (b) [1] Mr = 60 → C₃H₈O (A1). (c) [2] IHD = 0 (A1); no rings or π bonds (A1). (d) [1] O–H (alcohols), C–O (1). (e) [2] 3 environments in ratio 6:1:1 match CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (R1); structure (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Chirality is the most important type of isomerism in medicine."
items.answer: Chirality is critical for drug action, but all forms of isomerism matter to medicinal chemists.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: enantiomers can have very different biological activities (thalidomide, ibuprofen); drug regulators require single-enantiomer testing. Arguments against: structural isomers have completely different properties too; cis-trans isomerism matters in fats and in drugs such as cisplatin. Supported judgement: Chirality is critical for drug action, but all forms of isomerism matter to medicinal chemists.

items.stem: What is the effect of a racemic mixture on plane-polarised light?
items.answer: no net rotation
items.markingKey: B. Equal and opposite rotations cancel.

items.stem: Which statement about structural isomers is correct?
options: They always have the same boiling point.
They can have different functional groups and different chemical properties.
items.answer: They can have different functional groups and different chemical properties.
items.markingKey: C. e.g. ethanol and methoxymethane.

items.stem: "Enantiomers have different chemical properties in all reactions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Enantiomers react identically with non-chiral reagents; they differ only with other chiral species and in their effect on plane-polarised light.
items.markingKey: Enantiomers react identically with non-chiral reagents; they differ only with other chiral species and in their effect on plane-polarised light. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw and name the structural isomers of C₄H₉Cl.
items.answer: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane
items.markingKey: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane

items.stem: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₃H₆O₂ (consider only carboxylic acids and esters)?
items.markingKey: C. 3: propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate and ethyl methanoate (acids and esters only).

items.stem: Determine whether aminoethanoic acid, H₂NCH₂COOH, can exist as enantiomers. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No – no carbon atom is bonded to four different groups, so its mirror image is superimposable.
items.markingKey: No (1); reason: no carbon atom is bonded to four different groups, so its mirror image is superimposable. (1).

items.stem: Compound Y, C₄H₈, decolourises bromine water. (a) Draw and name all the structural isomers of Y that are alkenes. (b) Identify which one shows stereoisomerism and draw its two forms. (c) Explain why this isomerism occurs. (d) Y reacts with HBr to give a product with a chiral carbon. Suggest the identity of Y and of the product.
items.answer: (a) but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene. (b) but-2-ene: cis (Z) and trans (E). (c) restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups on each C. (d) but-1-ene or but-2-ene → 2-bromobutane (chiral C2).
items.markingKey: (a) but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene. (b) but-2-ene: cis (Z) and trans (E). (c) restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups on each C. (d) but-1-ene or but-2-ene → 2-bromobutane (chiral C2).

items.stem: Which absorption range (cm⁻¹) indicates a C=O bond?
items.markingKey: D. Data booklet.

items.stem: Why does CO₂ absorb infrared radiation although it is a non-polar molecule?
options: Its asymmetric stretching and bending vibrations change the dipole moment.
Its symmetric stretch changes the dipole.
items.answer: Its asymmetric stretching and bending vibrations change the dipole moment.
items.markingKey: C. IR activity needs a change in dipole.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why only some molecules absorb infrared radiation.
items.answer: A bond vibration absorbs IR only if it changes the dipole moment of the molecule; symmetrical vibrations of non-polar bonds (e.g. in N₂, O₂) do not absorb. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A bond vibration absorbs IR only if it changes the dipole moment of the molecule; symmetrical vibrations of non-polar bonds (e.g. in N₂, O₂) do not absorb. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The mass spectrum of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane shows a peak at m/z = 31. Which ion is most likely responsible?
items.answer: CH₂OH⁺
items.markingKey: A. m/z 31 corresponds to CH₂OH⁺ (data booklet fragments).

items.stem: State the m/z values of two fragments expected in the mass spectrum of ethanol and identify the ions.
items.answer: 31 (CH₂OH⁺), 29 (C₂H₅⁺); also 45 (M − H) or 15 (CH₃⁺)
items.markingKey: 31 (CH₂OH⁺), 29 (C₂H₅⁺); also 45 (M − H) or 15 (CH₃⁺)

items.stem: Freya writes: "The number of peaks in a ¹H NMR spectrum equals the number of hydrogen atoms." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Peaks correspond to different hydrogen environments; the integration ratio gives the relative number of H atoms in each.
items.markingKey: Peaks correspond to different hydrogen environments; the integration ratio gives the relative number of H atoms in each. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An unknown compound contains C 54.5 %, H 9.1 %, O 36.4 % by mass. Its mass spectrum has M⁺ at m/z = 88; its IR spectrum shows a strong absorption at 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad band above 2500 cm⁻¹; its ¹H NMR spectrum has three peaks with integration ratio 3:2:3 (singlet, quartet, triplet). (a) Determine the empirical and molecular formulae. (b) Deduce the functional group. (c) Deduce the structure.
items.answer: (a) C₂H₄O; C₄H₈O₂. (b) C=O with no O–H: ester. (c) CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, ethyl ethanoate (CH₃CO singlet, OCH₂ quartet, CH₃ triplet).
items.markingKey: (a) C₂H₄O; C₄H₈O₂. (b) C=O with no O–H: ester. (c) CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, ethyl ethanoate (CH₃CO singlet, OCH₂ quartet, CH₃ triplet).

items.stem: "Spectroscopic techniques have made traditional chemical tests obsolete." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Spectroscopy dominates structure determination, but chemical tests keep a role where speed, cost and portability matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: spectroscopy is fast, needs tiny samples and gives detailed structures; it is non-destructive (IR, NMR). Arguments against: instruments are expensive and need trained operators; simple tests (bromine water, Tollens’) are cheap, quick and portable; tests remain valuable for teaching and field work. Supported judgement: Spectroscopy dominates structure determination, but chemical tests keep a role where speed, cost and portability matter. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The breaking of a molecular ion into smaller positive ions and neutral species in a mass spectrometer"?
items.answer: fragmentation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of fragmentation.

items.stem: Explain why the ¹H NMR spectrum of propanone shows only one peak.
items.answer: All six hydrogens are in identical environments (two equivalent CH₃ groups attached to C=O), so they all absorb at the same chemical shift.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: All six hydrogens are in identical environments (two equivalent CH₃ groups attached to C=O), so they all absorb at the same chemical shift. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between low-resolution ¹H NMR and high-resolution ¹H NMR.
items.answer: Low resolution shows one peak per environment with areas in the ratio of H atoms; high resolution also shows splitting (n + 1 rule) revealing neighbouring hydrogens.
items.markingKey: Low resolution shows one peak per environment with areas in the ratio of H atoms; high resolution also shows splitting (n + 1 rule) revealing neighbouring hydrogens. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between IR absorption of an alcohol O–H and IR absorption of a carboxylic acid O–H.
items.answer: An alcohol O–H gives a broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; an acid O–H gives a very broad band at lower wavenumber, 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, often overlapping C–H.
items.markingKey: An alcohol O–H gives a broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; an acid O–H gives a very broad band at lower wavenumber, 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, often overlapping C–H. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which absorption, in cm⁻¹, would be present in the infrared spectrum of propanone but absent from that of hexane?
items.markingKey: C. propanone is a ketone: C=O 1700–1750; the alkane shows only C–H (2850–3090).

items.stem: What is the ratio of the peak areas in the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane?
items.answer: 9 (single peak)
items.markingKey: A. (CH₃)₃CBr: 1 environment(s), 9 (single peak).

items.stem: An unknown compound has the molecular formula C₃H₆O (molecular ion at m/z = 58). Its IR spectrum shows absorptions at 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR spectrum has 3 signals with areas in the ratio 3:2:1. Deduce the structure and name of the compound.
items.answer: propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
items.markingKey: IR: C=O → aldehyde (1); 3 environments in ratio 3:2:1 (1); structure CH₃CH₂CHO – propanal (1).

items.markingKey: (a) [2] Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest (M1); C₂H₄O (A1). (b) [1] Mr = 88 → C₄H₈O₂ (A1). (c) [2] IHD = 1 (A1); one π bond or ring (A1). (d) [1] C=O, C–O (1). (e) [2] 3 environments in ratio 3:2:3 match CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ (R1); structure (A1).

items.stem:
An unknown compound X has the percentage composition by mass: C 22.0 %, H 4.6 %, Br 73.3 %. The following spectroscopic data were obtained.

Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak at m/z = 109.
Infrared spectrum: only absorptions near 2900 cm⁻¹.
¹H NMR: 2 signals, integration ratio 3:2.

(a) Determine the empirical formula of X. [2]
(b) Use the mass spectrum to deduce the molecular formula of X. [1]
(c) Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of X and state what it indicates. [2]
(d) Identify the bond(s) responsible for the infrared absorptions. [1]
(e) Deduce the structure of X, explaining how the ¹H NMR data support it. [2]
items.answer: (a) C₂H₅Br (b) C₂H₅Br (c) 0 (d) C–H only (e) bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest (M1); C₂H₅Br (A1). (b) [1] Mr = 109 → C₂H₅Br (A1). (c) [2] IHD = 0 (A1); no rings or π bonds (A1). (d) [1] C–H (1). (e) [2] 2 environments in ratio 3:2 match CH₃CH₂Br (R1); structure (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "condensed structural formula"?
options: An alcohol in which the carbon bonded to the –OH group is attached to only one other carbon atom
A formula showing the groups attached to each carbon in order along the chain, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH
Stereoisomers that differ in the positions of groups relative to a double bond or ring, which restricts rotation
items.answer: A formula showing the groups attached to each carbon in order along the chain, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH
items.markingKey: C. "condensed structural formula" is a formula showing the groups attached to each carbon in order along the chain, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "tetramethylsilane (TMS)".
items.answer: The reference compound, Si(CH₃)₄, assigned δ = 0 ppm in ¹H NMR spectroscopy
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the reference compound, Si(CH₃)₄, assigned δ = 0 ppm in ¹H NMR spectroscopy. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "tertiary halogenoalkane".
items.answer: A halogenoalkane in which the carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to three other carbon atoms
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a halogenoalkane in which the carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to three other carbon atoms. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why are cis- and trans-but-2-ene not interconverted at room temperature?
options: Breaking the π bond to allow rotation requires a large amount of energy.
items.answer: Breaking the π bond to allow rotation requires a large amount of energy.
items.markingKey: C. Restricted rotation.

items.stem: "In a skeletal formula, the hydrogen of an –OH group is also omitted." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Only hydrogens bonded to carbon are omitted; the H of –OH (and N–H) is always shown.
items.markingKey: Only hydrogens bonded to carbon are omitted; the H of –OH (and N–H) is always shown. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does the molecular ion of chloromethane give two peaks, at m/z 50 and 52?
options: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
Carbon has two isotopes in equal amounts.
items.answer: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
items.markingKey: C. 3:1 isotope ratio.

items.stem: A student claims: "Benzene is unsaturated so it behaves like an alkene." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Benzene’s π electrons are delocalised, making it much more stable; it usually undergoes substitution, not addition.
items.markingKey: Benzene’s π electrons are delocalised, making it much more stable; it usually undergoes substitution, not addition. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why but-2-ene exists as cis and trans isomers but but-1-ene does not.
items.answer: Rotation about C=C is restricted by the π bond; in but-2-ene each double-bond carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃), but in but-1-ene one carbon carries two identical H atoms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rotation about C=C is restricted by the π bond; in but-2-ene each double-bond carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃), but in but-1-ene one carbon carries two identical H atoms. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the name of an ester has two parts.
items.answer: An ester is formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid; the alkyl group from the alcohol is named first and the carboxylate (-oate) from the acid second, e.g. ethyl ethanoate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An ester is formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid; the alkyl group from the alcohol is named first and the carboxylate (-oate) from the acid second, e.g. ethyl ethanoate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mateo writes: "The tallest peak in a mass spectrum is always the molecular ion." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The tallest peak is the base peak, often a stable fragment; the molecular ion is the peak at the highest m/z (excluding isotope peaks).
items.markingKey: The tallest peak is the base peak, often a stable fragment; the molecular ion is the peak at the highest m/z (excluding isotope peaks). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol and butan-1-ol as primary, secondary or tertiary.
items.answer: butan-2-ol secondary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol tertiary; butan-1-ol primary
items.markingKey: butan-2-ol secondary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol tertiary; butan-1-ol primary

items.stem: A pure sample of one enantiomer of 1,2-dibromopropane rotates plane-polarised light by +15.1° under certain conditions. A mixture of the two enantiomers under the same conditions rotates the light by +10.6°. Calculate the percentage of the (+) enantiomer in the mixture.
What is the molecular formula of ethanenitrile?
items.answer: C₂H₃N
items.markingKey: C. CH₃CN → C₂H₃N.

items.stem: Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of C₆H₆ and interpret it.
items.answer: IHD = (2 × 6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 4: one ring + three C=C (benzene)
items.markingKey: IHD = (2 × 6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 4: one ring + three C=C (benzene)

items.stem: A member of the alkenes has a molar mass of 42.09 g mol⁻¹. Using the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, determine the number of carbon atoms and write its molecular formula.
items.answer: 3 C atoms; C₃H₆
items.markingKey: Mr of general formula in terms of n set equal to 42.09 (M1); n = 3 (A1); C₃H₆ (A1).

items.stem: A pure sample of one enantiomer of 2-aminopropanoic acid rotates plane-polarised light by +35.8° under certain conditions. A mixture of the two enantiomers under the same conditions rotates the light by −14.3°. Calculate the percentage of the (+) enantiomer in the mixture.
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Systematic IUPAC names should completely replace common names in chemistry."
items.answer: IUPAC names are essential for precision, but common names will remain alongside them for convenience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each name corresponds to one structure – unambiguous worldwide; names can be deduced from structures and vice versa. Arguments against: names of large molecules become very long and impractical; common names (acetone, aspirin) are entrenched in industry and medicine; trade names are needed for products. Supported judgement: IUPAC names are essential for precision, but common names will remain alongside them for convenience.

items.stem: "Spectroscopic techniques have made traditional chemical tests obsolete." Discuss.
items.answer: Spectroscopy dominates structure determination, but chemical tests keep a role where speed, cost and portability matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: spectroscopy is fast, needs tiny samples and gives detailed structures; it is non-destructive (IR, NMR). Arguments against: instruments are expensive and need trained operators; simple tests (bromine water, Tollens’) are cheap, quick and portable; tests remain valuable for teaching and field work. Supported judgement: Spectroscopy dominates structure determination, but chemical tests keep a role where speed, cost and portability matter. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Classifying organic compounds by functional group is more useful than classifying them by carbon skeleton." Discuss.
items.answer: Functional groups predict chemistry best, but a full description needs both classifications.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: functional group determines reactivity, so reactions can be predicted; IUPAC naming is organised around functional groups. Arguments against: carbon skeleton determines physical properties, isomerism and shape; polyfunctional molecules belong to several classes. Supported judgement: Functional groups predict chemistry best, but a full description needs both classifications. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Molecular formulae are of little use in organic chemistry because of isomerism." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Molecular formulae are an essential first step, though never sufficient on their own.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many isomers share a formula (C₆H₁₄ has 5); a formula gives no structural information. Arguments against: molecular formula fixes Mr and composition, the starting point for structure determination; combined with IHD and spectroscopy it narrows possible structures. Supported judgement: Molecular formulae are an essential first step, though never sufficient on their own. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₃?
items.answer: propanone
items.markingKey: B. Ketone with three carbons.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fragmentation"?
options: The reference compound, Si(CH₃)₄, assigned δ = 0 ppm in ¹H NMR spectroscopy
The breaking of a molecular ion into smaller positive ions and neutral species in a mass spectrometer
An alcohol in which the carbon bonded to the –OH group is attached to only one other carbon atom
items.answer: The breaking of a molecular ion into smaller positive ions and neutral species in a mass spectrometer
items.markingKey: C. "fragmentation" is the breaking of a molecular ion into smaller positive ions and neutral species in a mass spectrometer.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "aromatic"?
options: A representation showing how the atoms in a molecule are bonded to one another
An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarised light
Containing a benzene ring (delocalised π system of six electrons)
Containing at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond
items.answer: Containing a benzene ring (delocalised π system of six electrons)
items.markingKey: C. "aromatic" is containing a benzene ring (delocalised π system of six electrons).

items.stem: A student claims: "Every molecule with a C=C double bond shows cis-trans isomerism." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not.
items.markingKey: Each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does propan-2-ol need a number in its name while ethanol does not?
options: In propanol the –OH can be on more than one distinct carbon, giving isomers.
Numbers are only used for secondary alcohols.
Ethanol has no isomers at all.
items.answer: In propanol the –OH can be on more than one distinct carbon, giving isomers.
items.markingKey: A. Locant distinguishes position isomers.

items.stem: Explain the n + 1 rule in high-resolution ¹H NMR.
items.answer: A signal is split into n + 1 lines by the n hydrogens on adjacent carbon atoms, because their spins can align with or against the field in different combinations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A signal is split into n + 1 lines by the n hydrogens on adjacent carbon atoms, because their spins can align with or against the field in different combinations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an amide and an amine.
items.answer: An amine has N bonded to carbon and hydrogen (–NH₂); an amide has the nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl carbon (–CONH₂).
items.markingKey: An amine has N bonded to carbon and hydrogen (–NH₂); an amide has the nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl carbon (–CONH₂). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between optical isomerism and cis-trans isomerism.
items.answer: Cis-trans isomerism arises from restricted rotation (C=C or ring); optical isomerism arises from a chiral centre with four different groups.
items.markingKey: Cis-trans isomerism arises from restricted rotation (C=C or ring); optical isomerism arises from a chiral centre with four different groups. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
items.answer: Both C₃H₇OH: in propan-1-ol the –OH is on the end carbon (primary); in propan-2-ol it is on the middle carbon (secondary).
items.markingKey: Both C₃H₇OH: in propan-1-ol the –OH is on the end carbon (primary); in propan-2-ol it is on the middle carbon (secondary). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: What is the index of hydrogen deficiency (IHD) of a compound with molecular formula C₃H₆O₂?
items.markingKey: C. IHD = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 for C₃H₆O₂ = 1 (rings + π bonds).

items.stem: State the name of the functional group present in HCOOCH₂CH₃ and the class of compound.
items.answer: ester group (–COO–); ester
items.markingKey: ester / –COO– (1); ester (1).

items.stem: Which of 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, 2-chloropentane, aminoethanoic acid and propan-2-ol has a chiral carbon atom?
items.answer: 2-chloropentane
items.markingKey: D. 2-chloropentane (CH₃CHClCH₂CH₂CH₃) has a carbon bonded to four different groups; the others do not.

items.stem: Which is the correct systematic name for the compound CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃?
items.answer: pentane
items.markingKey: B. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃: alkane → pentane.

items.stem: The mass spectrum of ethyl methanoate shows a peak at m/z = 29. Which ion is most likely responsible?
items.answer: C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺
items.markingKey: A. m/z 29 corresponds to C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺ (data booklet fragments).

items.stem: A member of the aldehydes has a molar mass of 72.12 g mol⁻¹. Using the general formula CₙH₂ₙO, determine the number of carbon atoms and write its molecular formula.
items.answer: 4 C atoms; C₄H₈O
items.markingKey: Mr of general formula in terms of n set equal to 72.12 (M1); n = 4 (A1); C₄H₈O (A1).

items.stem: Deduce whether 3-methylpent-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, shows cis-trans isomerism. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Yes – rotation about C=C is restricted and each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups.
items.markingKey: Yes (1); reason: rotation about C=C is restricted and each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups. (1).

items.stem: Two compounds, P and Q, both have the molecular formula C₄H₈O. P is an aldehyde and Q is a ketone. (a) Draw a structural formula and give the IUPAC name for a possible structure of P and of Q. (b) Determine the empirical formula of P. (c) State the type of isomerism shown. (d) Suggest one physical property that would differ between P and Q and explain why.
items.answer: (a) P butanal (CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO), Q butanone (CH₃COCH₂CH₃); (b) C₄H₈O; (c) structural isomerism (functional group); (d) e.g. boiling point – different intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: (a) correct structures and names, e.g. butanal and butanone (A1 A1 A1 A1). (b) C₄H₈O (A1). (c) structural (functional group) isomers (A1). (d) boiling point or solubility differs because of different intermolecular forces (e.g. hydrogen bonding in one) (R1).

items.stem:
An unknown compound X has the percentage composition by mass: C 52.1 %, H 13.2 %, O 34.7 %. The following spectroscopic data were obtained.

Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak at m/z = 46.
Infrared spectrum: 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (broad), 1050–1410 cm⁻¹ (strong).
¹H NMR: 3 signals, integration ratio 3:2:1.

(b) Use the mass spectrum to deduce the molecular formula of X. [1]
(c) Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency of X and state what it indicates. [2]
(d) Identify the bond(s) responsible for the infrared absorptions. [1]
(e) Deduce the structure of X, explaining how the ¹H NMR data support it. [2]
items.answer: (a) C₂H₆O (b) C₂H₆O (c) 0 (d) O–H (alcohols), C–O (e) ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH

items.stem: "Chirality is the most important type of isomerism in medicine." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Chirality is critical for drug action, but all forms of isomerism matter to medicinal chemists.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: enantiomers can have very different biological activities (thalidomide, ibuprofen); drug regulators require single-enantiomer testing. Arguments against: structural isomers have completely different properties too; cis-trans isomerism matters in fats and in drugs such as cisplatin. Supported judgement: Chirality is critical for drug action, but all forms of isomerism matter to medicinal chemists.
